content.transcript: My name is Salman Nasser and I'm in the air-wing of the police. I'm a helicopter pilot. My job is to help people in trouble. For example, someone may be very ill. He may be a long way from a hospital in a place where a car or ambulance can't get to him. Helicopters can go almost anywhere and they can get there very quickly. So I am sometimes able to save lives. If things like these didn't happen, I'd be out of a job - a job that I love.

activities.title: Serving the People
activities.instruction: Reading time! 📖 Read carefully and the texts from four people who serve the public. Then answer the questions to check your understanding.
activities.compensates: Replaces teacher-led 'Read for gist' activity (Teacher Guide, step 1). Allows for individual pacing and self-assessment.

content.passage:
Issa Said, Traffic Policeman: My job is to make roads safe for all road users. Most motorists obey the rules of the road. But some do stupid things and this makes them a danger to themselves and others. Cyclists and pedestrians can be silly too. If everybody obeyed the rules, our roads would be much safer.

Ali Abdullah, Immigration Officer: I work at the airport. My job is to check people entering and leaving the country by examining their passports. First-time visitors sometimes have problems with the regulations. I try to help them as much as I can. I am always polite and treat every person with respect.

Salman Nasser, Helicopter Pilot: I'm in the air-wing of the police. My job is to help people in trouble, for example, someone who is very ill in a place where an ambulance can't go. Helicopters can go almost anywhere very quickly, so I am sometimes able to save lives.

Fuad Rashid, Fireman: My job is to put out fires. My job is dangerous because fires can be extremely dangerous. Some accidents happen because people are careless. If people were more careful, there would be fewer fires.

activities.title: The History of Yemenia
activities.instruction: Reading time! 📖 Read carefully and the text about the Yemenia airline, then answer the questions below.
activities.compensates: Teacher-led activity to scan texts for specific information and check answers (Teacher Guide 2A & 2B).

content.passage: YEMENIA began flying on 1st January, 1961. In those days, it was a domestic airline. Its base was in Taiz and it flew to places like Aden, Hodeidah, Barat and Sana'a. It also flew to Djibouti and Asmara. The planes were DC-3s. Today, Yemenia is a modern international airline. It uses modern planes like the Boeing 727 and 737. In March 1997, Yemenia bought two Airbus 310 planes. These are among the most advanced planes in the world. On Yemenia, you can fly in comfort to the Gulf, Asia and Europe.

pairs.right: A word with the same or a similar meaning is used.
A word with the opposite meaning is used.
The word's meaning is directly explained in the sentence.
Specific examples are given to clarify the word's meaning.
The word is understood by its relationship to a cause or result.
The word is explained by what it does or what it is used for.
The word's meaning can be found by looking at its parts (prefixes, suffixes, root words).

activities.title: Decoding Newspaper Headlines
activities.instruction: Use your eyes! 🧐 Look closely at the at the newspaper headlines in the image. Answer the questions about their meaning.

options.feedback: While a boxer fights, 'weds' is related to the word 'sweetheart'.
Correct! 'Weds' is a shortened form of 'to wed', which means to marry.
This is possible, but 'weds' is a more specific and formal action.
This does not fit the context with 'sweetheart'.

questions.question: In the headline 'Boxer Weds Sweetheart', what does 'weds' most likely mean?
questions.explanation: The word 'weds' means marries. The clue is 'sweetheart', which refers to someone you love and would marry. This is an example of using cause and effect or context to understand a word.

options.feedback: 'Over' means finished, so the heat has ended.
Correct! If a heat wave is 'over', it means the period of very hot weather has finished.
'Over' indicates a change has happened.
While possible, the most direct meaning is that the heat has ended.

questions.question: The headline 'Heat Wave Over' suggests that the weather has become...
questions.explanation: In headlines, 'over' means 'finished'. So, 'Heat Wave Over' means the period of extremely hot weather has ended, and the temperature is now cooler.

options.feedback: The headline explicitly states '220 Dead'.
'No survivors' means nobody was rescued alive.
Correct. 'No survivors' is a synonym for 'everyone died'.
The headline says there was a crash and 220 people died.

questions.question: What can you infer from the headline '220 Dead in Air Crash: No Survivors'?
questions.explanation: The phrase 'No Survivors' is a direct explanation that clarifies the outcome of the crash: everyone involved died.

options.feedback: Correct! The fireman's quote, 'I'm extremely tired,' provides a synonym or explanation for 'exhausted'.

options.text: Meaning: brave. Clue: Cause and Effect.

questions.question: The firemen were <u>exhausted</u> after fighting the fire. ‘I’m extremely tired,’ one said. What does 'exhausted' mean and what clue helps you?

options.text: Meaning: mistakes. Clue: Cause and Effect.

activities.title: Grammar: Reporting the News (Passive Voice)
activities.instruction: News reports often use the passive voice to emphasize the action, not who did it. Rewrite the active sentences below into the passive voice.
activities.compensates: Teacher-led grammar explanation and practice on the passive voice.

sentences.original: The Romans built a giant dam nearly 2,000 years ago.
sentences.explanation: The object 'a giant dam' becomes the subject. We use 'was built' (past simple passive) because the action happened in the past.
sentences.transformed: A giant dam was built by the Romans nearly 2,000 years ago.

sentences.original: The authorities will demolish the old castle.
sentences.explanation: The object 'the old castle' becomes the subject. We use 'will be demolished' (future simple passive). We can omit 'by the authorities' as it's obvious.
sentences.transformed: The old castle will be demolished.

sentences.original: A rescue team rescued two swimmers from the sea.
sentences.explanation: The object 'two swimmers' becomes the subject. We use 'were rescued' (past simple passive).
sentences.transformed: Two swimmers were rescued from the sea.

sentences.original: Bird-watchers have seen a black stork in this country.
sentences.explanation: The object 'a black stork' becomes the subject. We use 'has been seen' (present perfect passive) because the original sentence is in the present perfect.
sentences.transformed: A black stork has been seen in this country.

content.passage: Every day, people enter the country by road, sea and air. Everybody who is not a citizen of this country must do two things. First, they must fill in a landing card. This tells me a lot about them - where they come from, what their jobs are, why they have come here, and so on. If they didn't fill in this card, we wouldn't know who was in the country. The second thing that they must do is show their passports. In fact, everybody must do this. Passports tell me a lot about people, including the countries they have visited. Every passport must contain a photograph of the owner. Some people must have a visa in their passports. This means that they have special permission to enter the country. If everything is correct, I stamp their passports and wish them a pleasant stay in my country.

content.transcript: Interviewer: Where were you exactly when the accident happened? Witness: I was in the baker's. I was buying a cake for my little daughter. It was her birthday. Interviewer: And you saw the accident. Witness: No. I heard the accident. There was a terrible crash and ran out of the shop. Interviewer: And what did you see? Witness: Two cars - a black one and a yellow one - had crashed into each other. Well, the yellow car had crashed into the black one. From behind. By the roundabout. Because of the fog, I suppose. You could hardly see your hand in front of your face. The two drivers were standing in the road, shouting at each other. And there was someone in the black car - hurt she was screaming. Then the police arrived - and the ambulance. Interviewer: Whose fault was it? Witness: The driver of the yellow car. I think. I think it was his fault. It looked as if he'd been driving too fast for the weather. But I don't know - I didn't see it, you see.

content.transcript: Interviewer: How do you feel now? Ed Shaw: Great. I nearly died, but I feel great now. Mrs Shaw: He felt awful. But he's better now. Interviewer: How long were you in hospital? Mrs Shaw: He was in there nearly a whole week. And the nurses were wonderful. Ed Shaw: Honey, it was four days. Not a week. Mrs Shaw: Well, four days, then. A long time, anyway. Interviewer: And what happened exactly? Ed Shaw: In the hospital? Interviewer: Er, no. What happened when you collapsed? Mrs Shaw: I told him to wear a hat. Just that morning I'd said; Honey, don't forget your hat. It's gonna be hot today; And what did he say? 'It never gets hot in England. This isn't California; And what happens? He falls ... Ed Shaw: Honey, can you let me explain? We went for a walk in the hills - those hills over there - and it was fine. Ok, the sun was shining, but there was a slight breeze - a very pleasant gentle wind - and it didn't feel hot. Mrs Shaw: But then we stopped at a restaurant and where did he want to sit? Outside! Outside in the sun. He knows he can't stand the heat and where does he want to sit? Outside. Ed Shaw: Honey! Please. We stopped for lunch and, yes, we sat outside in the garden of this restaurant - it was her idea - and there was ... Mrs Shaw: It was NOT! You said ... Ed Shaw: Anyway, we sat in the garden, and there was no wind, and the sun got hotter, and I didn't notice, and the next thing I knew I was in hospital. Mrs Shaw: He just collapsed. Right in the middle of lunch. He didn't even finish it. I just telling him that he was looking a bit strange when he just closed his eyes and fell off the chair. Well, I tell you, I was worried. He'd never done that before. But the people in the restaurant were marvellous. They called the ambulance and two hours Later we were in the hospital. He'd had a small heart attack. The doctor said ... Ed Shaw: The doctor said I was Ok but just needed a rest and some peace and quiet. Peace and quiet - fat chance!

content.transcript: Number 1. Air-hostess: Sameera, can you help me, please? Can you get a newspaper or a magazine for the man in Seat 17C? I have to get an orange juice for the woman in 22A. Number 2. Booking clerk: Gulf Air! Sorry, sir, we don't fly to Jeddah on Fridays. Saturday? Yes, sir. We have a flight leaving at 10.30 in the morning, arriving Jeddah at 12.55. I'll check, sir. Yes, sir, we have seats available on that flight. Of course, sir. Could you give me your name, please? Number 3. Engineer: Yousif! I have to look at the Airbus that's just arrived from Kuwait. The pilot isn't happy. Number 1 engine is giving trouble. Something about an oil leak! Can you carry on here? I'll be back as soon as I can. Number 4. Check-in clerk: Good morning, madam. May I have your ticket, please? Thank you. Is this all your luggage? Woman passenger: Yes. Check-in clerk: Smoking or non-smoking? Woman passenger: Non-smoking, please. Check-in clerk: This is your boarding card, madam. The flight leaves from Gate 7. We'll be calling passengers at 11.10. Have a nice flight. Woman passenger: Thank you. Number 5. Pilot: Alpha, Foxtrot, Charlie, 107 to control. Over! Air-traffic controller: Come in, 107. Over. Pilot: We've reached our cruising height of 33,000 feet. I will maintain my present altitude on a course of 235 degrees as instructed. Over. Air-traffic controller: Roger, 107. Have a good flight. Over and out. Pilot: Take over, please, Zuhair. I'm going back to have a word with the passengers. Co-Pilot: OK, captain. I've got control. Number 6. Chief chef: The menu for the morning flight to London is chicken kebab or fried hamour with rice or potatoes. Yousif, will you prepare the chicken, please? Ali, will you see to the fish dish?

questions.question: From his tone of voice, what does Jim think of Don's dream?

content.transcript:
Don: I had a dream last night. Well, a nightmare, actually.
Jim: Really? What about?
Don: It was awful. I was terrified. There were men with horrible faces and...
Jim: Just a minute. Calm down. Begin at the beginning. Now ... Where were you?
Don: I dreamt that we were working in the fields and ...
Jim: Who was? Who were you with?
Don: My brother. My elder brother. We were planting seed for next year. And I was driving the tractor. And it was brilliant weather. Then suddenly ...
Jim: Slow down. Slow down. What happened?
Don: I heard somebody shouting. Then I saw two men running towards us.
Jim: Who were they?
Don: I don't know. But they were really scary. One was holding a gun. My brother and I wanted to run but we couldn't move. It was terrible.
Jim: So how did you escape?
Don: I woke up.

content.passage:
I'm Fuad. I want to tell you about my sister and two friends of mine.

Fatma is my young sister. She is short and very slim. She is 1 metre 10 centimetres tall and weighs 27 kilos. She has got long black hair and brown eyes. She works very hard at school and she is very good at Arabic. She quite likes English too. She is very helpful. She likes working in the garden at the weekend.

Ali is one of my friends. He is quite short and a bit fat. He is 1 metre 55 and weighs 63 kilos. Some of my friends say he is rude, but that is not true. He has got a bad memory, so he forgets things people say to him. Ali is also a bit lazy. He likes motor bikes and he is good at fixing them. He wants to buy a motor-bike, but he does not have enough money.

Hassan is another friend. He is the opposite of Ali. He is tall and slim. He is 1 metre 78 and he weighs 60 kilos. He has got a good memory and he is very hard-working. He does not like cars or motor-bikes. He likes animals and birds, so he goes walking in the mountains at the weekend. He also likes photography, so he takes his camera with him. His favourite bird is the black stork.

activities.title: Two Journeys: Ahmed and Paul
activities.instruction: Reading time! 📖 Read carefully and the texts about Ahmed Said and Paul Archer from Pupil's Book page 9, then answer the questions below.
activities.compensates: Digitizes the reading comprehension exercises WB2.5A and WB2.5B.

content.passage:
Ahmed Said was born in Taiz. He is one of seven children. At secondary school his best subjects were English and history. As a student he listened to the radio, watched TV and read every newspaper he could get his hands on. Then he went to Sana'a University. He took a degree in journalism. He has worked as a journalist for two years. Now, at the age of twenty-five, he is going to England to continue his studies at Exeter University.

Exeter is a city in the south-west of England. When I asked Ahmed why he had chosen Exeter, he said, "Exeter is about the same size as Sana'a. It has a local newspaper, TV station and radio station. It brings news to ordinary people in the area. They tell people what is happening in their area. That's what I am interested in and that's what I want to do. London is too big. That's why I didn't want to go there."

---

Paul Archer was born in Manchester. He is one of three children. At secondary school his best subjects were mathematics and history. As a student he was interested in buildings, old and new. Then he went to Cardiff University. He took a degree in architecture. He has worked as an architect for twenty-five years. Now, at the age of fifty, he is going to Sana'a. He will work with Yemeni architects restoring old buildings.

When I asked him why he had chosen Sana'a, he said, "The old buildings in Sana'a are wonderful. There is nothing like them anywhere in the world. I will learn a lot and maybe I can help a little bit. That's why I want to go there."

activities.title: Metaphorical Meanings
activities.instruction: The underlined words are used metaphorically. Challenge yourself! 📝 Select the best option for the correct meaning for each sentence. This is based on Workbook activity B.
activities.compensates: Workbook activity B on page 5 and the related class discussion.

options.feedback: This is the literal meaning, not the metaphorical one.

options.text: It received a very large number of calls.
options.feedback: Correct! It was overwhelmed by the quantity of calls, like a flood.
The word 'flooded' here refers to quantity, not quality.
A flood is usually fast and overwhelming.

questions.question: In the sentence 'The radio station was _flooded_ with telephone calls,' what does 'flooded' mean?
questions.explanation: To be 'flooded' with something means to receive so much of it that it's difficult to manage.

options.feedback: While the news might be sad, the metaphor refers to how it spread.

options.text: The news was about a fire.
options.feedback: The fire is used as a comparison for speed.
Excellent! Forest fires spread very rapidly, so this means the news traveled fast.
This metaphor doesn't comment on the truth of the news.

questions.question: What does 'like a forest fire' mean in the sentence 'The news of the Princess's death spread around the country _like a forest fire_.'?
questions.explanation: The phrase 'like a forest fire' is a simile used to describe something that spreads very quickly and is hard to control.

options.feedback: A hurricane is the opposite of quiet and slow.

options.text: Very quickly and with a lot of energy.
options.feedback: Correct! A hurricane is a powerful and fast-moving storm, so this describes energetic movement.
While hurricanes spin, the metaphor focuses on speed and force.
The metaphor describes the manner of movement, not the time.

questions.question: In 'The headteacher rushes around the school _like a hurricane_,' how does the headteacher move?
questions.explanation: Comparing someone to a 'hurricane' suggests they are moving with great speed, force, and energy.

activities.title: From Headlines to Sentences
activities.instruction: Newspaper headlines are often written in a short style. Rewrite these headlines as complete sentences. This is based on Workbook activity C.
activities.compensates: Workbook activity C on page 4.

sentences.original: Victim of Road Accident Dies
sentences.explanation: Headlines often omit articles ('a', 'the') and auxiliary verbs ('has'). We need to add them to make a full sentence.
possible_answers: A victim of a road accident has died.
The victim of the road accident has died.

sentences.original: 220 Dead in Air Crash: No Survivors
sentences.explanation: We need to add a verb ('are' or 'have died') and expand the second part into a full clause.
possible_answers: 220 people are dead in an air crash and there are no survivors.
Two hundred and twenty people have died in an air crash and there were no survivors.

sentences.original: Thick Fog to Clear by Afternoon, Then Sun
sentences.explanation: The infinitive 'to clear' in a headline suggests a future event. We can use 'is expected to' or 'will'.
possible_answers: The thick fog is expected to clear by the afternoon, and then there will be sun.
Thick fog will clear by the afternoon, followed by sun.

activities.title: Listen to Ahmed's Journey
activities.instruction: Listen carefully! 🎧 Clear your ears and to the audio about Ahmed's flight from buying a ticket to landing. Then, answer the questions.

questions.question: What time did Ahmed's flight leave?

content.transcript: Agent: Good afternoon, sir. Ahmed: Good afternoon. I'd like a ticket to London, please. Agent: We have a flight on Sunday at 08:15. It arrives in London Gatwick at 16:00. Ahmed: That's fine. I'll take the Sunday flight. [scene change] Agent: Good morning, sir. Is this all your luggage, sir? Ahmed: Yes, just one suitcase and one piece of hand luggage. Agent: Smoking or non-smoking? Ahmed: Non-smoking, please. Agent: Window or aisle? Ahmed: I'd like a window seat, please. Agent: Here's your boarding card, sir. Row 16, seat A. Have a pleasant flight. [scene change] Announcement: Will passengers with seats in rows 14 to 29 please board now? [scene change] Flight Attendant: What would you like to eat, sir? Ahmed: I'd like the chicken and some fruit, please. [scene change] Captain: Good afternoon, ladies and gentlemen. This is your Captain speaking. We are now flying at 33,000 feet and our speed is 580 miles per hour. As you can see, the weather is fine and, if you are sitting near a window, you will soon have a beautiful view of the mountains of Eastern Turkey. [scene change] Ahmed: Excuse me! May I have an apple juice, please? Flight Attendant: I'm sorry sir. We haven't got any apple juice. Would you mind having orange juice? Ahmed: No, not at all. [scene change] Announcement: We are about to land at London Gatwick where the time is 16.00 exactly. It is raining in London and there is quite a strong wind, but the temperature is fifteen degrees Celsius. Will you please fasten your seat belts and put out your cigarettes? Thank you.

activities.title: Reading: A Journey's Details

activities.compensates: Replaces teacher-led 'Read for detail' questioning from the Teacher Guide.

content.passage:
**Buying a ticket**
Agent: Good afternoon, sir.
Ahmed: Good afternoon. I'd like a ticket to London, please.
Agent: We have a flight on Sunday at 08:15. It arrives in London Gatwick at 16:00.
Ahmed: That's fine. I'll take the Sunday flight.

**Checking in**
Agent: Good morning, sir. Is this all your luggage, sir?
Ahmed: Yes, just one suitcase and one piece of hand luggage.
Agent: Smoking or non-smoking?
Ahmed: Non-smoking, please.
Agent: Window or aisle?
Ahmed: I'd like a window seat, please.
Agent: Here's your boarding card, sir. Row 16, seat A. Have a pleasant flight.

**Enjoying the view**
Captain: Good afternoon, ladies and gentlemen. This is your Captain speaking. We are now flying at 33,000 feet and our speed is 580 miles per hour. As you can see, the weather is fine and, if you are sitting near a window, you will soon have a beautiful view of the mountains of Eastern Turkey.

**Landing at London**
Announcement: We are about to land at London Gatwick where the time is 16.00 exactly. It is raining in London and there is quite a strong wind, but the temperature is fifteen degrees Celsius.

content.transcript:
Police Officer: Good afternoon, how can I help you?
Visitor: Hello. I'm afraid I've lost my camera. I would like to report it missing.
Police Officer: Of course. Could you tell me your name, please?
Visitor: Yes, it's Fatima Al-Ali.
Police Officer: Thank you, Ms. Al-Ali. And where did you last see the camera?
Visitor: I think I left it on a bench in the central park, about an hour ago. It's a black digital camera.
Police Officer: Okay, I'll take down the details. Could you give me a contact number, please? We'll call you if it's found.
Visitor: Yes, it's 555-0123. Thank you for your help.
Police Officer: You're welcome.

activities.title: Making Polite Requests
activities.instruction: Reading time! 📖 Read carefully and the impolite sentences. Rewrite them to make them polite. Use phrases like 'Could you...', 'Would you mind...', or 'I would like...'.
activities.compensates: Replaces the teacher-led activity WB2.6B, transforming impolite statements.

sentences.original: Give me my bag.
sentences.explanation: Adding 'Could you please' or 'Would you mind' makes the request polite instead of a command.
possible_transformations: Could you please give me my bag?
Excuse me, I think that's my bag. Would you mind passing it to me?
I would be grateful if you could give me my bag.

sentences.original: Tell me the time.
sentences.explanation: Starting with 'Excuse me' and using a question form like 'Could you' is a common polite pattern.
possible_transformations: Could you please tell me the time?
Excuse me, do you have the time?
Would you mind telling me the time?

sentences.original: I want a new one.
sentences.explanation: 'I would like...' is a much more polite way to express a desire than 'I want...'.
possible_transformations: I would like a new one, please.
Could I possibly have a new one?
I was wondering if it would be possible to get a new one.

activities.title: Role Play: At the Police Station
activities.instruction: You have lost your wallet. You are at the police station to report it. Challenge yourself! 📝 Select the best option for the most polite and appropriate responses to have a conversation with the police officer.
activities.compensates: Replaces the teacher-led pair work and role play from WB2.6C, providing a guided, self-paced digital alternative.

turns.text: Good morning. How can I help you?
turns.speaker: Police Officer

studentOptions.text: I would like to report a lost wallet, please.
studentOptions.feedback: Great! That's a very polite way to start.

studentOptions.text: I lost my wallet. Give me a form.
studentOptions.feedback: This is a bit impolite. Try using 'I would like to...' or 'Could you please...'.

turns.text: I'm sorry to hear that. Could you please tell me your full name and address?
turns.speaker: Police Officer

studentOptions.text: Of course. My name is [Your Name] and I live at [Your Address].
studentOptions.feedback: Perfect. Providing the information clearly is very helpful.
It's better to cooperate. The police need this information for their report.

turns.text: Thank you. And can you describe the wallet and what was inside?
turns.speaker: Police Officer

studentOptions.text: Yes, it's a brown leather wallet. It had my ID card and about 100 riyals inside.
studentOptions.feedback: Excellent, a clear description is very important.

studentOptions.text: It's just a wallet. You find it.
studentOptions.feedback: Try to be more specific. The more details you give, the better the chance of finding it.

turns.text: Okay, I've filed the report. We will contact you if we find anything. Is there anything else?
turns.speaker: Police Officer

studentOptions.text: No, that's all. Thank you very much for your help.
studentOptions.feedback: A perfect way to end the conversation politely.
It's more polite to thank the officer for their time and help.

content.transcript:
Ali: What time does the bus leave?
Fuad: Let’s see. Er, twelve minutes to ten.
Ali: And how long does it take to get to the bus station?
Fuad: About twenty minutes. Yes, twenty minutes.
Ali: So we need to get there at nine-thirty.
Fuad: No, Ali. That’s too late. We have to buy our tickets. I’d like to get to the station at ten past nine at the latest.
Ali: Oh, all right. We’ll get to the bus station at ten past nine.

activities.title: Listening: An Interview with Abla
activities.instruction: Listen carefully! 🎧 Clear your ears and to the interview with Abla Saeed. Then, answer the questions.
activities.compensates: Workbook exercise 2.7A, which requires listening to a cassette (CS3) and writing short answers.

questions.question: How old is Abla Saeed?
What is her job?
Where does she work?

content.transcript: Reporter: I'm a policewoman. You work at the airport, Abla, don't you? Abla: That's right. I work in security. Reporter: What exactly do you do? Abla: Everybody who goes on a plane must be checked. It's my job to search ladies' hand luggage. I must make sure that there is nothing dangerous in their bags. Reporter: How do you do that? Abla: All the bags are X-rayed. If we see anything we're not sure of, we open them. Reporter: So, it's a very responsible job? Abla: Yes, it is. It means that you have to be very careful all the time. You can't relax. Reporter: What do you do after work? Abla: Watch TV. Visit my friends. Reporter: What do they think about your job? Abla: They tease me. They tell me I'm too small to be a policewoman. Reporter: And your family? Abla: They think it's great. In fact, it was my mother who suggested that I join the police. Reporter: So you enjoy your job? Abla: Very much. I enjoy the responsibility. I make people feel safe. That makes me feel good. Reporter: Any ambitions? Abla: Yes. I'd like to continue with my education and maybe join the air-wing. Reporter: So you'll stay in the police? Abla: Definitely. If I left the police, I wouldn't be happy.

sentences.text: If you look in the top drawer, you ___ your keys. (see)

sentences.text: If I had his phone number, I ___ him. (meet)
sentences.explanation: The 'if' clause is in the past tense ('had'), so this is an unlikely situation (Type 2). We use 'would meet'.

sentences.text: If I were you, I ___ more careful. (be)
sentences.explanation: This is an impossible situation used for giving advice (Type 2), so we use 'would be'.

sentences.text: If he ___ less, he would be healthier. (eat)
sentences.explanation: The result clause uses 'would be', so the 'if' clause must be in the past tense for a Type 2 conditional. The answer is 'ate'.

sentences.text: If I ___ to London, I would visit the British Museum. (go)
sentences.explanation: The result clause 'I would visit' indicates a Type 2 conditional, so the 'if' clause needs the past tense verb 'went'.

activities.instruction: Reading time! 📖 Read carefully and the text about Fuad Rashid's job as a fireman and answer the questions that follow. This is from page 11 of your Pupil's Book.

content.passage:
Fuad Rashid is a fireman. Here, he is talking about the work of the fire brigade.

Putting out fires is not the only thing we do in the fire brigade. We give advice on fire prevention and we give advice on what to do if there is a fire. We are often called to traffic accidents to help the traffic police. And then there are the unexpected jobs, all different.

Helping at traffic accidents is another part of our job. Maybe the car is on fire. We put it out. Sometimes people are trapped in the car and we have to cut them free. This often makes me angry because a lot of accidents are unnecessary. They are caused by bad driving.

Giving advice is an important part of our job. We check buildings and point out things that could start a fire. We also make sure that there are enough fire extinguishers. We make recommendations about safety equipment such as fireproof doors and smoke-alarms. In a burning building, smoke can be as dangerous as fire, so we tell people what to do about smoke. We also carry out fire-drill practice.

Last week, we were called to a house. A little boy had been saying goodbye to his father when he put his head through the bars of the gate and couldn't get it out again. We had to bend the bars to free him. It's all part of the job. In the fire brigade, we have to be ready for the unexpected.

questions.question: In the sentence 'The school bus had left when Hassan arrived at the bus stop', which event happened first?

activities.title: Present Perfect vs. Past Simple
activities.instruction: Reading time! 📖 Read carefully and each sentence and complete it with the correct tense of the verb in brackets. Use either the Present Perfect or the Past Simple.
activities.compensates: This is a digital, self-correcting version of Workbook Activity A on page 5.

content.feedback: Great effort! You've successfully completed the sentences. Keep it up! 🚀

sentences.text: Over the years there ___ (to be) many disastrous volcanic eruptions.
sentences.explanation: We use the Present Perfect ('have been') because 'Over the years' indicates a period of time that continues up to the present.

sentences.text: The worst ___ (to take place) in Krakatoa in 1883.
sentences.explanation: We use the Past Simple ('took place') because a specific past time ('in 1883') is mentioned.

sentences.text: Over 36,000 people ___ (to lose) their lives.
sentences.explanation: This event is part of the 1883 eruption, so we use the Past Simple ('lost').

sentences.text: A large passenger plane ___ (to crash) in the mountains.
sentences.explanation: We use the Present Perfect ('has crashed') to describe a recent event with a present result (the plane is still crashed, rescue is ongoing).

sentences.text: So far rescue teams ___ (to find) no survivors.
sentences.explanation: The phrase 'So far' indicates a period up to the present, so we use the Present Perfect ('have found').

sentences.text: The plane ___ (to take off) from London two days ago.
sentences.explanation: We use the Past Simple ('took off') because a specific past time ('two days ago') is mentioned.

sentences.text: The pilot ___ (to contact) Jeddah airport one hour before the plane crashed.
sentences.explanation: This action happened at a specific time before another past event, so we use the Past Simple ('contacted').

sentences.text: Several people ___ (to die) recently as a result of traffic accidents.
sentences.explanation: 'Recently' often signals the use of the Present Perfect ('have died') for recent past events with present relevance.

sentences.text: Last Thursday two small children ___ (to be) killed by a speeding car.
sentences.explanation: We use the Past Simple ('were') because a specific past time ('Last Thursday') is mentioned.

activities.title: Combining Sentences with Relative Clauses
activities.instruction: Combine the two sentences into one using a relative clause. Remember to place the preposition correctly.
activities.compensates: This activity provides interactive practice for the concepts in Pupil's Book page 15, section 3, and is based on Workbook Activity B.

prompts.prompt: Combine these sentences: The bus has had an accident. I come to school on it.
prompts.explanation: This is a relative clause with necessary information, so the preposition 'on' goes at the end of the clause. No commas are needed.
correct_answers: The bus I come to school on has had an accident.

prompts.prompt: Combine these sentences: The Great Fire of London happened in 1666. Thousands of buildings were destroyed in it.
prompts.explanation: This is a relative clause with additional information. The preposition 'in' moves to the beginning of the clause with 'which'. The clause is placed between commas.
correct_answers: The Great Fire of London, in which thousands of buildings were destroyed, happened in 1666.

prompts.prompt: Combine these sentences: The man has mysteriously disappeared. I was talking to him yesterday.
prompts.explanation: This is a relative clause with necessary information. The preposition 'to' goes at the end of the clause. No commas are needed.
correct_answers: The man I was talking to yesterday has mysteriously disappeared.

prompts.prompt: Combine these sentences: The Armenian earthquake killed over 25,000 people. I have to write about it in the next lesson.
prompts.explanation: This is a relative clause with additional information. The preposition 'about' moves to the beginning of the clause with 'which'. The clause is placed between commas.

prompts.prompt: Combine these sentences: The flood of 1953 is still the worst in living memory for the people of The Netherlands. New dams were built after it.

activities.title: Reading: The Eruption of Krakatoa
activities.instruction: Reading time! 📖 Read carefully and the passage about the historic eruption of Krakatoa and answer the comprehension questions.

content.passage: History has recorded many disastrous volcanic eruptions, but few have been as powerful as the one that occurred in Krakatoa. The eruption, which took place in 1883, was one of the most violent volcanic events in modern history. The explosion was so loud that people heard it nearly 5,000 kilometers away. For months after the event, strange weather patterns affected the entire globe. The eruption and the tsunamis it created caused immense destruction. In the immediate aftermath, over 36,000 people lost their lives. The island of Krakatoa, in which the volcano was located, almost completely disappeared. Scientists today continue to study the event to better understand volcanic activity. The area, to which researchers now travel frequently, has become a living laboratory for studying how life recolonizes a devastated landscape.

activities.instruction: Reading time! 📖 Read carefully and the text from page 12 of your Pupil's Book about how to make a garden. Then, answer the questions.

content.passage: First, dig the soil to break it up. You can do this with a spade or a fork. This is hard work! Next, give the soil some food to make your plants grow well. You can buy artificial fertilizer, or maybe you can get natural fertilizer from a farm. It is called manure. You can dig the fertilizer into the soil, or put it on top. Now you can plant your seeds. Give them plenty of water, but use a watering can. A hose will wash the seeds away. When the young plants appear, they need a lot of water. Water them in the evening when the sun is not very hot. Weeds will also grow in your garden and they will kill your plants. Use a hoe to get rid of weeds.

questions.question:
Read the article below. Which is the best headline?

Fire completely destroyed a school in Salah yesterday. When the fire-engines arrived from nearby Taiz, the fire was blazing out of control. 'We couldn't save the school. But we pointed our hoses at the houses next to the school,' said Fireman Rashid, 'and we saved them.' One fireman was injured and had to be rushed to hospital.

questions.question:
Read the second article. Which is the best headline?

A fireman from Taiz ran into the flames of a blazing school yesterday evening to save the caretaker, who was asleep. The fireman's hands were badly burned and he is now in hospital. Luckily the caretaker was not injured. The fire completely destroyed the primary school in Salah. Two fire-engines rushed to the scene from nearby Taiz, but the fire was already out of control. However, the fire brigade were able to save the houses next to the school. Fireman Fuad Rashid said the fire was probably started by an electrical fault.

correctOrder: 13.00: Flash. Earthquake in Armenia. The town of Spivak at 11.41 local time. 6.9 on the Richter scale. First reports say that damage is serious.

14.00: Armenia: Considerable loss of life reported. 'The buildings were very badly built,' said an eye-witness. 'They fell down like packs of cards.' The rescue workers have no equipment and are working with their bare hands.

15.00: Armenia: Spivak completely flattened. Most of population - 20,000 - killed. In Leninakan, Armenia's largest city, thousands of people are homeless. One in five of buildings destroyed. 'We urgently need tents and blankets,' a spokesman said.

16.00: Earthquake Epidemic Risk: Rescue workers say there is a danger of cholera and typhoid following the Armenian earthquake. 'There is no clean drinking water,' said a nurse. 'Disease can spread very quickly. We need clean water now.'
17.00: Earthquake: The Armenian earthquake is the strongest since 1964 when an earthquake measuring 8.6 on the Richter scale hit Alaska.
23.00: President to return: President Gorbachov is interrupting his trip to the USA to take charge of rescue efforts. Officials number of dead 55,000. Some say this could reach 100,000.

sentences.transformed: A spokesman said that they urgently needed tents and blankets.

sentences.original: 'The buildings were very badly built,' said an eye-witness.
sentences.explanation: The past simple 'were' changes to the past perfect 'had been' in reported speech.
sentences.transformed: An eye-witness said that the buildings had been very badly built.

sentences.original: 'There is no clean drinking water,' said a nurse.
sentences.explanation: The present tense 'is' changes to the past tense 'was' in reported speech.
sentences.transformed: A nurse said that there was no clean drinking water.

sentences.original: 'Disease can spread very quickly,' she added.
sentences.explanation: The modal verb 'can' changes to 'could' in reported speech.
sentences.transformed: She added that disease could spread very quickly.

Boat: No. Nothing. We haven’t seen anything. Over!
HQ: What is your position? Where are you now? Over!
Boat: We’re about 20 kilometres south of Zinjibar. Over!
HQ: What’s the weather like? What’s the weather like? Over!
Boat: It’s bad. Quite bad. And it’s getting worse. There’s a strong wind blowing from the north east. Over!
HQ: Can we do anything? Can we help? Over!
Boat: Yes. Yes, you can. A helicopter would help. Repeat. A helicopter. It’ll be dark in two hours. We must find that fishing boat before then. We’ve got to. Over!

content.passage: First, dig the soil to break it up. You can do this with a spade or a fork. This is hard work! Next, give the soil some food to make your plants grow well. You can buy artificial fertilizer, or maybe you can get natural fertilizer from a farm. It is called manure. You can dig the fertilizer into the soil, or put it on top. Now you can plant your seeds. Give them plenty of water, but use a watering can. A hose will wash the seeds away. When the young plants appear, they need a lot of water. Water them in the evening when the sun is not very hot. Weeds will also grow in your garden and they will kill your plants. Use a hoe to get rid of weeds.

content.passage:
Hassan is seventeen. His favourite school subject is history because he is interested in Yemen's past. He also loves animals. Every Friday he goes walking in the mountains. He takes photographs of birds and animals. He has a lot of photographs of foxes and hares, but he has only one of a gazelle. He saw it in the Hijaz. Laila is eighteen. Her favourite school subjects are physics and chemistry. She is interested in helping people. She is very kind and friendly. On Fridays, she visits a hospital. Some patients have no visitors. Laila takes flowers to these patients and she sits and talks with them. Laila is going to work in a hospital, but first she has to go to university.

content.passage:
It was five o'clock in the evening when we reached Dubai. We had left Bahrain three hours earlier. The plane landed on the clear water of the Creek and taxied to the landing stage. Three cars were waiting for us.

Fifteen minutes later we were driving along the bumpy road to the fort at Sharjah. It was a magnificent building with huge iron doors and a large courtyard. I hurried to my room, had a quick wash and then watched the desert sunset. It was a sight that I will never forget.

Later in the evening a wedding party from Sharjah arrived. Soon music, laughter and the smell of delicious food filled the courtyard. A smiling man in a long, white thobe came up to me and said, 'Come! Join us. Be our guest.' I did, and I had a wonderful time.

The next morning we were driven back to the Creek. I sat back in my seat as the plane lifted off the water. I had spent a very short time in the country, but I had met some wonderful people. I decided to come back some day.

content.transcript:
Reporter: Yousif, thank you for speaking with us. First of all, how are you feeling?
Yousif: I'm tired, but I'm so grateful to be alive.
Reporter: Can you tell us what happened? Where were you when the storm hit?
Yousif: We were about 50 kilometers from the coast. The weather changed so suddenly. The waves were huge, it was terrifying.
Reporter: Did you have any food or water on the boat?
Yousif: We had some, but it ran out after two days. We survived by catching rainwater.
Reporter: How did you manage to stay hopeful?
Yousif: We prayed. We never gave up hope that we would be found.
Reporter: And finally, what's the first thing you want to do now that you're back on land?
Yousif: I just want to see my family and hug my children.

content.transcript:
Reporter: What was the weather like then?
Yousif: Not bad. We knew it might get worse, but bad weather doesn't worry us.
Reporter: What happened this time? What went wrong?
Yousif: Well, we were about fifteen kilometres south-east of Shuqrah when the engine stopped. And it wouldn't start again. The weather was getting worse. The wind was much stronger and it was blowing from the north-east.
Reporter: Blowing you farther out to sea?
Yousif: That's right. But there was nothing we could do. No engine. No sail.
Reporter: Were you worried?
Yousif: Of course we were worried. But we knew that somebody would be looking for us. So we just sat in the boat and waited for them to find us.
Reporter: Did you have any food in the boat?
Yousif: Yes. We had some coffee, some bread and some dates.
Reporter: How did you find when the police found you?
Yousif: How did we feel? What do you think?

activities.title: Saved! The Full Story
activities.instruction: Reading time! 📖 Read carefully and the newspaper article from Pupil's Book page 14 and answer the questions.
activities.compensates: Replaces teacher-led reading and comprehension questions (PB14 Text Study).

content.passage:
Early on Tuesday morning a fishing boat left the village of Shuqrah. The three men on board were Yousif Hassan, his brother, Kamal, and his cousin, Omar. According to Yousif Hassan, the weather was reasonable at the time. They set off towards the fishing grounds, thirty kilometres south of Shuqrah, but they never reached them. About fifteen kilometres out, their engine died. When this had happened on previous occasions, Kamal had always been able to find the fault and repair it. This time, however, the engine was beyond repair. There was nothing they could do except wait to be rescued. As the north-easterly wind grew stronger, they were blown farther and farther out to sea.

Late on Tuesday night when the three men had not returned, their worried families called the police. The next morning a police boat began looking for the missing fishing boat. They searched all day without success. At five o'clock the weather was getting worse and the police asked for help from the air-wing. A police helicopter joined the search and one hour later the pilot, Salman Nasser, found the missing boat. He guided the police boat on his radio and waited until it arrived. The police boat threw a rope to the fishermen and headed back to Shuqrah with the boat in tow. Five hours later, the three men were back with their families. Yousif Hassan told me that although they had begun to get a little worried, they were confident that the police rescue team would find them eventually.

options.feedback: Great! Remember: Present Perfect is for an unknown time in the past. Past Simple is for a specific, known time.

questions.question: Study this rule from your workbook before you start.
questions.explanation: We use the Present Perfect (have/has + past participle) to talk about actions in the past when the time is not specific. We use the Past Simple to talk about actions that happened at a specific time in the past (e.g., yesterday, last week, in 2010).

activities.title: Reading: The Snake (Part 1)
activities.instruction: Reading time! 📖 Read carefully and the story from Pupil's Book page 14 and answer the questions below.
activities.compensates: Replaces teacher-led reading aloud and comprehension questions (PB14).

content.passage:
Hassan shook his young brother. 'Get up, Khalid,' he said. 'It's quarter past seven.'
'Go away. 'It's too early to get up,' said Khalid.
'OK. I'll see you when I get back,' said Hassan. 'I'm going to look for a black stork.'
Khalid sat up. 'Can I come?' he shouted.
'Yes, you can. I'm going to make some sandwiches,' Hassan replied.

Half an hour later, the two boys left the house. Hassan was carrying his camera. His brother was carrying a plastic bag with food and water in it.
'What does a black stork look like?' asked Khalid.
'It's a big, beautiful bird,' said Hassan. 'It lives in Africa for half the year and it lives here for the other half.'
'Is it here now?' Khalid asked.
'I don't know,' Hassan replied. 'We'll see.'

'Hassan, it's half past ten,' said Khalid.
'I know,' replied Hassan. 'So what?'
'I'm tired and hot. I'm hungry and thirsty too,' replied Khalid.
'All right,' said Hassan, smiling. 'We'll stop here for a little bit.'
They sat down next to a rock. Hassan handed his brother a sandwich.
Khalid bit into it.
'It's beautiful here,' said Khalid.
'Yes, it is,' replied Hassan. 'The mountains are wonderful.' Suddenly, he put his hand on Khalid's arm.
'Look!' he whispered.
Khalid looked up.
'It's a falcon,' said Hassan quietly. 'Now, watch.'
The falcon suddenly fell out of the sky like a stone. A few seconds later, it was up and flying again. It was carrying something.
'It looks like a hare,' said Hassan. 'There are lots of hares in the mountains. That's its lunch.'
'Hare for lunch - that's better than a cheese and tomato sandwich,' said Khalid.

sentences.prompt: Can you tell me when the game starts?
sentences.explanation: In a direct question with 'when', we use the auxiliary verb 'does' before the subject 'the game'.

sentences.prompt: Please explain why you are late.
sentences.explanation: In a direct question with 'why' and the verb 'to be', we invert the subject 'you' and the verb 'are'.

sentences.prompt: Do you know how far it is to the airport?
sentences.explanation: In a direct question with 'how far', we invert the subject 'it' and the verb 'is'.

sentences.prompt: I’d like to know what this word means.
sentences.explanation: In a direct question with 'what', we use the auxiliary verb 'does' before the subject 'this word'.

activities.title: Reviewing Past Tenses
activities.instruction: Reading time! 📖 Read carefully and the story. Fill in the blanks with the correct form of the verb in brackets (Past Simple, Past Continuous, or Past Perfect).

content.feedback: Great effort! You've successfully completed the sentences. Keep it up! 🚀

sentences.text: The fire started because someone ___ (drop) a cigarette.

blanks.hint: Which action happened first: the fire starting or the cigarette dropping?

sentences.explanation: We use the Past Perfect ('had dropped') because this action happened before the other past action ('the fire started').

sentences.text: When I arrived at the station, my uncle ___ (wait) for me in his car.

blanks.hint: Was this a long, continuous action or a short, completed one?

sentences.explanation: We use the Past Continuous ('was waiting') for an action that was in progress at a specific time in the past ('when I arrived').

sentences.text: While he was waiting, he ___ (listen) to a football match on the radio.
sentences.explanation: The Past Continuous ('was listening') describes a background action that was happening over a period of time.

sentences.text: My mother ___ (teach) me to cook when I was young.

blanks.hint: This is a completed action in the past.

sentences.explanation: We use the Past Simple ('taught') for a completed action at a general or definite time in the past.

activities.title: Past Perfect: Giving Reasons
activities.instruction: Reading time! 📖 Read carefully and the situation, then complete the explanation using the past perfect form of the verb in brackets. For example: '...because he (leave) his books' becomes '...because he had left his books'.
activities.compensates: The teacher-led group competition for past perfect practice.

content.feedback: Great effort! You've successfully completed the sentences. Keep it up! 🚀

sentences.text: Hamad didn't have his books yesterday because he ___ them at home.
sentences.explanation: We use the past perfect (had + past participle) to talk about an action that happened before another action in the past.

sentences.text: Huda couldn't eat her dinner because she ___ too many cakes in the afternoon.
sentences.explanation: First, Huda ate the cakes. Second, she couldn't eat her dinner. The earlier past action uses the past perfect.

sentences.text: Abdulla was very tired last night because he ___ football all afternoon.
sentences.explanation: Playing football happened before he was tired. We use the past perfect for the earlier action.

sentences.text: I couldn't find my keys because I ___ them in the car.
sentences.explanation: The action of forgetting the keys happened before the action of trying to find them.

sentences.text: By the time the plane took off, the sun ___.
sentences.explanation: The sun set before the plane took off. The past perfect is used for the action that was completed first.

activities.title: Making Polite Requests
activities.instruction: Read the response and Challenge yourself! 📝 Select the best option for the most appropriate polite request that someone probably asked.
activities.compensates: The Teacher Guide activity where students think of requests for given responses.

options.text: Do you mind if I open the window?
options.feedback: Correct. 'Not at all' is a common polite response to a 'Do you mind...?' question.
Incorrect. A more likely response to 'Can you...?' would be 'Yes, of course' or 'Sure'.
This is a question asking for a reason, not a request.

questions.question: Response: 'Not at all. Please, go ahead.'
questions.explanation: The phrase 'Do you mind if I...?' is a polite way to ask for permission. 'Not at all' means 'I don't mind'.

options.text: Do you like cleaning your car?
options.feedback: This is a question about preference, not a request for help.

options.text: Would it be possible for you to help me with my homework?
options.feedback: Correct. This is a polite request for help, and the response gives a reason for being unable to help.
The response answers this question, but it's not a request.

questions.question: Response: 'I'm sorry, I can't. I'm cleaning my car.'
questions.explanation: 'Would it be possible for you to...?' is a very polite way to ask someone to do something. The response 'I'm sorry, I can't' is a polite refusal with a reason.

options.text: Could you help me lift this heavy box?
options.feedback: Correct. This request involves physical effort, and hurting one's back is a good reason to refuse.

options.text: Would you mind telling me the time?
options.feedback: Incorrect. Telling the time doesn't require physical effort, so this response wouldn't make sense.

options.text: How did you hurt your back?
options.feedback: This is a question asking for information, not a request for action.

questions.question: Response: 'I'm sorry. I've hurt my back.'
questions.explanation: A polite request like 'Could you help me...?' can be refused politely by giving a valid reason, like an injury.

options.feedback: Correct! 'Bit' is the past tense of 'bite'.
Incorrect. 'Bite' is an irregular verb.

options.feedback: Incorrect. 'Shake' is an irregular verb.

options.feedback: Not quite. Remember the spelling rule for verbs ending in 'y'.

activities.title: Talking About the Future
activities.instruction: Read the situation and Challenge yourself! 📝 Select the best option for the best way to talk about the future.
activities.compensates: This activity replaces the teacher-led open-pair practice for future forms mentioned in the Teacher Guide for PB15.

options.feedback: We use the present continuous for fixed arrangements, not for sudden decisions.
Correct! We use 'will' for spontaneous decisions made at the moment of speaking.
We use 'going to' for plans made before speaking, not for a sudden decision.

questions.question:
A: The phone is ringing! 
B: Don't worry, I ___ it.
questions.explanation: Use 'will' for offers and spontaneous decisions.

options.feedback: This is a fixed plan, so another form is better.
Perfect! We use the present continuous ('are going') for fixed arrangements in the future.
This is the present simple, used for schedules, not personal arrangements.

questions.question: I have bought the tickets. We ___ to the cinema on Friday.
questions.explanation: Use the present continuous for future arrangements that are already confirmed (like buying tickets).

options.feedback: This form is not used to talk about future plans.
'Will' is for predictions without evidence. 'Going to' is better for intentions.
Correct! We use 'going to' to talk about our plans and intentions for the future.

questions.question:
A: What are your plans after you finish school? 
B: I ___ a doctor.
questions.explanation: Use 'going to' to talk about future plans and intentions.

content.prompt: Use the text above as a model. Write your own short story about buying a present. Remember to use the past simple and linking words like 'and', 'but', 'so', and 'then'.
content.initial_text: Ali wanted to buy a pair of earrings for his sister. He walked up the street and went into a jewellery shop. He looked at some earrings, but he didn’t like them, so he bought a ring.
content.example_answer: I wanted to buy a book for my brother. I walked to the town centre and went into a bookshop. I looked at some story books, but they were too expensive, so I bought a science magazine.

activities.title: Connecting the Story
activities.instruction: Challenge yourself! 📝 Select the best option for the correct linking word to connect the ideas in the sentences.
activities.compensates: Replaces teacher-led discussion about link words from WB2.16B.

options.feedback: Correct! 'And' is used to connect two similar ideas.
Not quite. 'But' is used to show a contrast.
Incorrect. 'So' is used to show a result.

questions.question: He looked left ___ right.
questions.explanation: We use 'and' to join two related actions: looking left, looking right.

options.feedback: Try again. Is the second idea similar or different?
Excellent! 'But' shows a contrast between looking at the earrings and not liking them.
Not quite. 'So' would mean not liking them was a result of looking at them.

questions.question: He looked at some earrings, ___ he didn’t like them.
questions.explanation: We use 'but' to connect two contrasting ideas. He looked, which is positive, but he didn't like them, which is negative.

options.feedback: Incorrect. Buying a ring is a result of not liking the earrings.
Try again. 'But' shows a contrast, but this is more of a result.
That's right! 'So' shows the result or consequence of an action.

questions.question: He didn’t like the earrings, ___ he bought a ring.
questions.explanation: We use 'so' to show that buying the ring was the result of not liking the earrings.

options.feedback: Incorrect. Looking left again is not a result.
Perfect! 'Then' is used to show the next action in a sequence.
Not quite. There is no contrast here, just a sequence of events.

questions.question: He looked left and right. ___, he looked left again.
questions.explanation: We use 'Then' to show the order of events in a story. First, he looked left and right. Next, he looked left again.
